output.title: Exception queues before automation
output.body:
Before you automate anything, name the exception queue first. That is the work that falls outside the main workflow: customer questions that need a different answer, invoice mismatches, data corrections, or other cases that interrupt the day. If you cannot point to the queue, automation usually stays fuzzy.

For one week, track three things for that queue: how many exceptions arrive, how long each one takes to resolve, and what rule the team uses to decide the outcome. Then sort the queue into three buckets: routine, mixed, or ad hoc. Routine exceptions are the clearest candidates for a narrow automation pilot. Mixed queues still need human review built in. Ad hoc work often stays manual, because the pattern is weak.

Keep the control rules visible while you do it. If the queue touches approvals, thresholds, audit trails, money movement, or other high-risk decisions, human sign-off stays in place. Automation can help organise the review, but it does not replace the person who has to own the decision.

If the data lives in email, spreadsheets, or someone’s head, clean that up first. A short inventory of one exception queue is often the most useful next step.
